slides.title: Era 1 — The Doordarshan Years
slides.subtitle: 1959–1990s · One nation, one channel
key_points: State-owned broadcasting
Limited hours, shared viewing
Culture-defining shows
slides.visual_hint: Full-bleed retro texture with a single CRT television silhouette glowing in the center; muted sepia palette

slides.title: Birth of Doordarshan
slides.subtitle: Television arrives in India
key_points: 1959 — Experimental telecast from Delhi
1976 — Doordarshan separates from All India Radio
1982 — Asian Games spark color TV & national expansion
One channel, evening-only slots, communal viewing
Shows became shared national rituals
slides.visual_hint: Left: archival photo of an early DD broadcast / families gathered around a TV. Right: small inset of the classic DD logo

slides.title: Doordarshan Milestones
slides.subtitle: The shows that defined a generation
key_points: 1976 — Doordarshan established
1982 — Color broadcast; Asian Games
1984–86 — Hum Log, Buniyaad (first soaps)
1986 — Mahabharat — Sunday morning phenomenon
1989 — Ramayan — streets would empty during airtime
slides.visual_hint: Horizontal timeline ribbon with milestone nodes; each node carries a small show title card / thumbnail
slides.layout_hint: horizontal timeline across full width, single row of nodes

slides.title: The DD Phenomenon
slides.subtitle: One screen, a nation glued
key_points: ~1 channel available for most households through the 80s
Ramayan (1987) — among most-watched shows globally at the time
Broadcast windows: evening slots only; no 24×7 TV
TV ownership grew from thousands to millions in the 80s
Content was family-viewing by necessity — appointment TV
slides.visual_hint: Stat grid: 3 large numeric tiles with captions + a simple line chart showing TV household growth 1980→1990
slides.layout_hint: 3-column stat tiles on top, mini-chart strip below

slides.title: Era 2 — Cable & Satellite
slides.subtitle: 1990s–2000s · The channel explosion
key_points: Private broadcasters arrive
Choice, genres and daily soaps multiply
TV becomes a 24-hour, multi-language medium
slides.visual_hint: Full-bleed image of a wall of TV screens / a cable dish skyline; shift to cooler, more saturated palette

slides.title: Doordarshan vs The Cable Era
slides.subtitle: Two models of television
key_points: Ownership: state monopoly → private + multi-broadcaster
Channels: 1–2 → hundreds, across languages
Scheduling: fixed evening slots → 24×7 programming
Genres: myth/soap/social → soaps, reality, news, music, kids
Audience: shared national viewing → fragmented, segmented
slides.visual_hint: Two-column comparison table with a center divider; left column tinted sepia, right column tinted blue

slides.title: Soaps, Stars & Sunday Blockbusters
slides.subtitle: The daily-fiction + reality boom
key_points: Kyunki Saas Bhi Kabhi Bahu Thi (2000) — era-defining daily soap
Kaun Banega Crorepati (2000) — reality/gameshow goes primetime
Indian idol, MTV, Channel V — youth & music programming
TRP race begins: ratings drive scheduling & budgets
Star, Zee, Sony, Colors reshape the competitive landscape
slides.visual_hint: Collage strip: soap set still, KBC hot-seat, music countdown graphics — three thumbnails in a row
slides.layout_hint: top: 3-image collage row; bottom: text bullets in single column

slides.title: Appointment Viewing
key_points: "In the cable era, families planned their evenings around the 9 PM soap."
slides.visual_hint: Full-bleed dimmed image of a living room around a CRT TV; large pull-quote centered, oversized opening quotation mark in accent color

slides.title: Era 3 — Digital & OTT
slides.subtitle: 2010s–present · The unbundling of TV
key_points: Internet and smartphones reach mass scale
Streaming platforms disaggregate the 'channel'
Binge, originals, regional and global content mix
slides.visual_hint: Full-bleed image of a smartphone + laptop streaming grid of show thumbnails; vibrant modern palette

slides.title: The Streaming Surge
slides.subtitle: India goes online, on-demand
key_points: 500M+ internet users in India by mid-2020s
Dozens of OTT platforms: Hotstar/JioHotstar, Netflix, Prime, ZEE5, SonyLIV, MX Player & more
Cheap mobile data: among the lowest rates globally → mass streaming
Originals & regional content expand sharply
Linear TV still large, but growth shifts to digital
slides.visual_hint: Dashboard: big-number tiles + a bar chart of digital viewership growth 2015→2025; small platform logos row
slides.layout_hint: top: 3 stat tiles; middle: bar chart; bottom: logo strip

slides.title: Linear TV vs OTT
slides.subtitle: Two ways to watch
key_points: Access: scheduled broadcast → on-demand streaming
Device: living-room TV → phone, tablet, laptop, TV
Model: channel bundle → subscription + freemium + AVOD
Content: censored, family-safe → originals, mature, regional, global
Control: broadcaster decides → viewer decides (pause, binge, skip)
slides.visual_hint: Side-by-side comparison table; left column 'Linear TV' with TV icon, right 'OTT' with play icon; center arrow showing the shift
slides.layout_hint: 2-column table with a directional arrow motif between headers

slides.title: The Full Arc, 1959 → 2025
slides.subtitle: Six decades on a single ribbon
key_points: 1959 — First experimental telecast
1982 — Color TV & Asian Games
1992–95 — Cable & satellite channels launch (Zee, Star, Sony)
2000 — Daily soaps + KBC redefine primetime
2015–20 — Mobile data + OTT platforms explode
2020s — Streaming originals, regional wave, live sports on OTT
slides.visual_hint: Long horizontal timeline spanning the full slide; era bands color-coded (sepia → blue → vibrant); milestone markers with mini icons
slides.layout_hint: full-width horizontal timeline, three era bands shaded beneath

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.subtitle: What the evolution tells us
key_points: From scarcity to abundance: one channel to infinite choice
From appointment viewing to on-demand control
From national consensus to fragmented, personal taste
From state gatekeeper to creator-led & platform-led economy
Constant: storytelling remains central — the screen just changed
